humanities_role_explanation: Historical documents (business letters, index cards, Fraktur newspapers, medieval manuscripts, library cards) supply the items, but the competence tested is document-processing: transcription, layout segmentation, structured metadata extraction, XML repair. These are generic pipeline skills applied to humanities sources, not interpretive disciplinary competence.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Most datasets are scanned page images (JPG) paired with prompts/schemas and structured JSON output; one dataset (Book Advert XMLs) is text-only (JSON files containing XML).
analytical_tasks_explanation: Tasks: transcription, page/advert segmentation, handwritten text recognition, metadata extraction, NER, person matching and signature recognition, and correction of faulty LLM-generated XML structure (described as a reasoning task). No interpretive or generative tasks.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Small, task-specific datasets focused on document-centred digital humanities workflows; explicitly not intended as generic leaderboard or representative of the humanities.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: OpenAI (gpt-4o, gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-5), Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5, Google Gemini (gemini-2.0-pro-exp) among others.

quantitative_metrics.note: Fuzzy matching, F1, character error rate, normalised to 0-100%.

summary: The paper presents a framework and eight small, expert-verified datasets drawn from real digital humanities projects, together with a provider-agnostic tool that runs LLMs against them and a web interface for results. It prioritises realism, reproducibility and transparency over scale, and tracks model performance over time.
key_findings: Best results per dataset range from 58.40% (Company Lists, gpt-5) to 97.47% (Book Advert XMLs, Claude Sonnet 4.5); Blacklist Cards 95.65%, Fraktur Adverts 95.70%, Library Cards 89.51%, Business Letters 77.00%, Medieval Manuscripts 76.90%, Bibliographic Data 71.43%. 633 test runs across 487 configurations. Scores are not comparable across datasets.
evaluation_unit: image (document page/card/letter) per dataset; one text-only dataset uses JSON files
facets_explanation: Ground truths were 'either manually produced or carefully verified by domain experts' within the RISE projects; validation focused on correctness with respect to task and schema. Answers are matched against a single key via fuzzy matching or F1. The paper says ground truth is 'operationalised scholarly interpretation' but does not discuss annotator disagreement.
results_explanation: The highest per-dataset best result is 'Best result 97.47%, Anthropic, Claude Sonnet 4.5' on Book Advert XMLs (fuzzy matching on whole XML string, normalised 0-100%). Metrics differ across datasets, so the headline is not comparable with others. No format gaps or human baseline are reported.

humanities_role.quote: such as transcription, layout segmentation, and structured metadata extraction from scanned historical sources

dataset_size.quote: 8 benchmark datasets (detailed in Table 1) and 2 test datasets.

primary_evaluation_setting.quote: using the defined prompt and schema, captures the model output, validates it against the schema

gold_source.quote: All ground truths were either manually produced or carefully verified by domain experts.
gold_source.where: p. 4, Quality control and ground truth validation

gold_beyond_stimulus.quote: Ground truths are subsequently created or verified by domain experts and represent the expected output for each source item.

answer_multiplicity.quote: Fuzzy matching on each key in the JSON items.
